the-attorney-2013.gazette: The Burim case began in Busan in 1981, when readers of banned books were held without warrants and confessions were taken under the National Security Act. Roh Moo-hyun, then a tax lawyer with no record in human rights work, took the defense and never returned to tax practice. The convictions were overturned on retrial in 2014, the year after the film opened.

the-conjuring-2013.gazette: The Perron family lived in a Rhode Island farmhouse in the early 1970s, and the eldest daughter, Andrea, later published a multi-volume memoir of what she says happened there. Ed and Lorraine Warren's case files, kept in their own archive, are the other main source, and skeptics have contested both accounts. Lorraine Warren consulted on the production.

the-lunchbox-2013.gazette: Mumbai's dabbawalas have carried home-cooked lunches across the city since the 1890s, by bicycle, handcart and suburban train, routed by painted codes rather than written addresses. Business schools, Harvard's among them, have written the network up as a study in near-zero error rates. The film's entire plot depends on one delivery reaching the wrong desk.
the-lunchbox-2013.prism: A system famous for never failing only becomes a story the moment it does. The film borrows the dabbawalas' reputation for precision and then spends two hours inside the exception, which is a strange kind of tribute and probably the only one available.

the-wolf-of-wall-street-2013.gazette: Stratton Oakmont operated out of a Long Island office in the 1990s, selling penny stocks by phone to investors who lost most of what they put up. Belfort cooperated with prosecutors, served under two years, and was ordered to pay restitution he has repeatedly been reported as behind on. He wrote the memoir the film adapts, and appears in it briefly, introducing the actor playing him.

spotlight-2015.gazette: The Boston Globe's Spotlight team published its first story on the Archdiocese in January 2002, built from sealed court files, settlement records and the paper's own clipping morgue. Cardinal Bernard Law resigned that December, and the reporting took the Pulitzer Prize for Public Service the following year. The cast shadowed the reporters they play, all of whom appear on screen under their own names.

o-j-made-in-america-2016.gazette: Ezra Edelman's film runs nearly eight hours across five parts, setting the 1995 trial inside decades of Los Angeles police history, from Watts in 1965 to the Simi Valley acquittals. Trial footage, archival news, and interviews with jurors, prosecutors and Simpson's own circle carry most of it. It won the Academy Award for Best Documentary Feature, after which the Academy changed its rules to bar multi-part television work.
o-j-made-in-america-2016.prism: The length is the argument. A shorter cut would have had to choose between the trial and the city that produced it, and the whole claim of the film is that they were never separable.

the-conjuring-2-2016.gazette: Between 1977 and 1979, in a council house in north London, the Hodgson children reported knocking, moving furniture and a voice claiming to belong to a dead man. Maurice Grosse and Guy Lyon Playfair of the Society for Psychical Research logged hundreds of hours of tape; the children later admitted faking some incidents, and investigators divided over how much of the rest held up. The Warrens, who are the film's investigators, spent only a brief stretch at the house.

beauty-and-the-dogs-2017.gazette: In 2012 a young woman in Tunis was raped by police officers and then charged with indecency by the same institution she had reported to; she published her account under a pseudonym. The officers were convicted, and an appeals court increased the sentences in 2014. Kaouther Ben Hania stages the aftermath as nine chapters, each an unbroken take, so the night moves at the speed of the paperwork.

molly-s-game-2017.gazette: Molly Bloom ran high-stakes private poker games in Los Angeles and later New York until a 2013 federal indictment swept her up alongside a Russian-American gambling ring. She pleaded guilty, drew probation and a fine rather than prison, and kept most of the players' names out of her book. Aaron Sorkin, directing for the first time, wrote her lawyer as a composite and left the court record standing.
molly-s-game-2017.prism: The commercial value of that memoir was the list of names, and she declined to sell it. So the film is built on a book whose central act is a refusal to disclose, which makes the withholding, not the poker, the actual plot.

godland-2022.gazette: The premise is seven wet-plate photographs recovered in Iceland, and the production actually made them: collodion negatives exposed on location with period equipment and the long, unforgiving times that method demands. Hlynur Pálmason shot on 35mm in a squared frame with rounded corners to match the plates. The crew walked the same southeastern routes the priest walks and came back across seasons to let the terrain change on camera.

the-northman-2022.gazette: The Northman descends from the Amleth story in Saxo Grammaticus's twelfth-century Gesta Danorum, the same source that eventually produced Hamlet. Robert Eggers wrote it with the Icelandic poet Sjón and worked with Viking Age archaeologists and historians on the buildings, weapons, ritual and Old Norse dialogue. Much of it was filmed in Northern Ireland on constructed turf-and-timber settlements rather than sets dressed to suggest them.

perfect-days-2023.gazette: The Tokyo Toilet project rebuilt seventeen public restrooms in Shibuya with architects including Tadao Ando, Kengo Kuma and Shigeru Ban, whose glass stalls turn opaque only once the door is locked. Wim Wenders arrived on a commission to make short films about the buildings and left with a feature about the man who cleans them. The restrooms on screen are the restrooms; nothing was built for the camera.
perfect-days-2023.prism: A public-works commission turned into a film about a man who owns almost nothing, and the sponsor got a better advertisement than it ordered. The catch is that the dignity on screen belongs to a job that pays badly in the real Shibuya, and the film is careful never to say so out loud.

the-holdovers-2023.gazette: The Holdovers opens on a vintage Focus Features logo and a ratings card in the old MPAA style, then sustains the illusion with grain, dust and reel-change cues burned into the corner of the frame. Alexander Payne and his crew engineered that wear deliberately in the grade, aging the image toward a well-used 1970s release print. The story sits in a New England boarding school over Christmas 1970, and the surface arrives before the plot does.

the-taste-of-things-2023.gazette: Trần Anh Hùng gives the first half hour almost entirely to cooking, with no score and little dialogue: a vol-au-vent, a pot-au-feu, a baked Alaska, worked through in sequence on a wood-fired range. Pierre Gagnaire designed the dishes and drilled the actors, who handle the knives themselves. Marcel Rouff's 1924 novel Dodin-Bouffant supplied both the French title and the period kitchen the film reconstructs.

late-night-with-the-devil-2024.gazette: The film presents itself as a recovered master tape of a live Halloween broadcast from 1977, intercut with black-and-white footage of what took place during the commercial breaks. The Cairnes brothers built the Night Owls set, graphics and camera language to period spec, shooting in Melbourne and holding long takes so the show reads as transmission rather than scene. The conceit is total: the picture never leaves the studio's own footage.
late-night-with-the-devil-2024.prism: It sold itself on hand-built period accuracy and then took sustained heat for three AI-generated interstitial images. Authenticity only works as a claim while it is complete; one visible seam and the audience starts hunting for the others.
